strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in natural-language-to-code generation: improving both functional correctness and hardware efficiency. Integrating simulation and synthesis feedback into model training is well motivated.

The method is clearly formulated, combining hierarchical evaluation, per-objective advantage normalization, adaptive process-reward weights, and preference-conditioned PPA objectives. Fail-fast evaluation also provides a practical computational benefit.

Reported improvements span four model families and multiple benchmarks. The SFT-only comparisons, individual reward ablations, and component ablations provide useful evidence that reinforcement learning contributes beyond data augmentation.

The additional experiments across process libraries, synthesis tools, and larger AutoSilicon designs strengthen the empirical scope and provide preliminary evidence of transfer beyond the training configuration.
weaknesses: The central PPA comparison does not control for differences in successfully solved tasks. Appendix C averages performance only over each model’s successful tasks, so models are evaluated on different design subsets. Best/worst scores also depend on how many valid candidates each model produces. Report paired comparisons on common successful tasks, coverage, and an end-to-end success measure incorporating PPA targets; the current aggregates do not establish the claimed magnitude of hardware-efficiency improvement.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the central hardware results. The manuscript omits essential EDA settings, including tool versions, timing and I/O constraints, power-activity assumptions, and the precise backend stage used for measurement. CDPO’s EMA coefficient, initial curriculum weights, functional-reward weight, and numerical preference templates are also unspecified. The abstract’s artifact statement has no link, while Appendix B promises a future release.

Preference following is not directly demonstrated. Comparing different models under selected optimization prompts, and reporting the best target metric across attempts, cannot distinguish controllable trade-offs from generally better generation. Evaluate the same designs under different preferences and report all resulting PPA components, correctness, and trade-off behavior. The preference-vector ablation is useful but does not resolve this issue.

The functional reward’s reliability is underexamined. Generated testbenches are conditioned on the reference implementation and retained when that implementation passes; this establishes consistency rather than independent correctness or adequate coverage. No mutation testing, coverage analysis, independent test suite, or equivalence-checking audit is reported. This matters particularly when optimization can exploit weak tests, although the external benchmark results do provide independent evidence of functional improvement.

Several reporting inconsistencies require reconciliation. Table 4 labels its functional metric Pass@1 while Section 4.3 describes pass@5. Base-model RTLLM-v2.0 pass@5 values differ between Tables 2 and 7 without an explained protocol change. Equations 13–14 define power×delay and power×delay×area but label them energy-delay and energy-delay-area products; under the usual energy=power×delay interpretation, these names imply an additional delay factor.

No repeated-run uncertainty or paired significance analysis is provided, despite the small RTLLM evaluation and several modest differences. The GRPO/DAPO comparisons also need explicit matching of training data, reward configuration, and computational budget. Taken together with the evaluation and reproducibility gaps, these concerns prevent a sound Findings recommendation in the current version, despite the promising contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in language-model code generation: improving hardware efficiency alongside functional correctness. Integrating compilation, simulation, synthesis, and PPA feedback into training is a coherent approach with practical value.

The reported improvements are substantial across four model backbones. For example, ChipSeek-QC achieves 84.09% pass@5 on RTLLM v2.0 versus 72.73% for GPT-o1, while reporting lower normalized PPA costs. VerilogEval results provide additional evidence beyond the hardware-efficiency benchmark.

The experimental coverage includes meaningful training-stage, reward-component, and CDPO-component ablations, plus comparisons with GRPO and DAPO. The additional PDK/toolchain sensitivity experiments and AutoSilicon evaluation strengthen the empirical case, although their reporting needs improvement.

The method is reasonably clear at the algorithmic level: equations and pseudocode explain component-wise advantage normalization, curriculum weights, and preference conditioning. The measured benefits of parallel evaluation and early termination also support the pipeline's engineering utility.
weaknesses: The central PPA comparisons do not control for differences in task coverage. Appendix C averages over each model's successfully generated tasks, so models are evaluated on different subsets; handling of functionally correct but unsynthesizable outputs is also unclear. Consequently, Table 2 does not establish the stated magnitude of hardware-efficiency improvement on comparable designs. Report paired comparisons on shared tasks, coverage counts, and an end-to-end measure incorporating failures.

The energy metrics are incorrectly named or defined. Equations 13–14 calculate power × delay and area × power × delay, respectively, but call these Energy-Delay Product and Energy-Delay-Area Product. Under the usual energy = power × execution-time interpretation, these omit an additional time factor. The paper must distinguish critical-path delay from execution time, define its intended objective, and correct the terminology or recompute the results; this can affect rankings and optimization conclusions.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the main hardware claims. Although Appendix B supplies several training settings, it omits numerical curriculum EMA and functional-reward weights, exact preference vectors, and sufficiently detailed EDA configurations, including timing constraints, power activity assumptions, tool versions, and implementation stages. Repository provenance and benchmark deduplication procedures are also underspecified. The abstract's artifact statement has no link, while Appendix B promises a future release.

Passing generated testbenches is treated too strongly as evidence of correctness. Training testbenches are generated from the reference code and retained when that code passes, which establishes agreement rather than independently validating the specification or test coverage. No mutation testing, coverage audit, or independent equivalence checks are reported. This does not invalidate the external benchmark results, but it leaves the reliability of the training reward and the semantic validity of aggressive PPA optimizations insufficiently established.

Several evaluation details and results require reconciliation. Table 4 labels correctness as Pass@1 while Section 4.3 calls it pass@5; baseline RTLLM v2.0 pass@5 values differ between Tables 2 and 7 without explanation. Training seeds, uncertainty estimates, baseline evaluation provenance, and the exact AutoSilicon subset are not adequately reported. These gaps particularly limit confidence in smaller component-ablation gains.

Claims of controllable trade-offs and production-level scalability exceed the evidence. Preference-specific best-of-five scores and the preference-vector ablation are useful, but do not directly demonstrate how changing preferences alters competing objectives for the same design. Likewise, average code length and aggregate AutoSilicon scores alone do not establish production readiness. Overall, the promising contribution needs corrected metrics, comparable PPA evaluation, and reproducible experimental specifications before a sound Findings recommendation; these are substantive but plausibly next-cycle revisions.

strengths: The paper addresses a valuable problem in natural-language-to-code generation: improving hardware efficiency alongside functional correctness. Integrating executable EDA feedback into model training is well motivated and relevant to NLP.

The method is coherent: hierarchical evaluation avoids unnecessary tool calls, component-wise advantage normalization addresses heterogeneous reward scales, and curriculum weighting provides a plausible mechanism for shifting training priorities.

Reported functional improvements are substantial across four base models and multiple benchmarks. The SFT-versus-RL comparisons in Tables 6–7 provide useful evidence that the gains extend beyond the initial supervised adaptation.

The experimental coverage is extensive, including reward and algorithm-component ablations, alternative PDKs and synthesis tools, larger AutoSilicon designs, and runtime measurements. These strengthen the empirical case beyond a single benchmark configuration.
weaknesses: The central PPA comparison is confounded by model-dependent task coverage. Appendix C averages PPA only over tasks successfully generated by each model, so models are evaluated on different subsets. Reporting correctness separately does not establish that the claimed relative PPA reductions hold on comparable designs. Common-task paired comparisons, coverage counts, and a joint correctness–efficiency measure are needed.

Important reproducibility details are missing despite the useful implementation appendix: numerical preference vectors, the functional-reward weight, EMA coefficient and initialization, SFT settings, and precise dataset sourcing/filtering procedures. The physical evaluation also lacks tool versions, synthesis scripts, timing constraints, power/activity assumptions, and handling of backend failures. These choices directly affect the principal results; the submission provides no usable artifact link.

The evidence for controllable trade-offs is incomplete. Better scores under separately targeted prompts do not establish that changing preferences reliably steers the same design between competing objectives. Table 8 provides a helpful preference-vector ablation, but matched-task preference sweeps and cross-objective measurements are needed to substantiate the stronger trade-off-navigation claims.

Functional validation of the synthetic training data relies on generated testbenches passing their source implementations. This establishes agreement, not test adequacy or specification correctness. No coverage, mutation-testing, independent audit, or equivalence evidence is reported. Benchmark simulation results remain useful, but stronger validation is particularly relevant when optimizing PPA against potentially incomplete tests.

Several reporting issues undermine confidence in the quantitative interpretation. Equations 13–14 define power×delay and area×power×delay while calling them energy-delay and energy-delay-area products. Table 4 labels correctness as Pass@1 while its discussion says pass@5, and its full-model EDAP differs from Table 8 without an explanation. Base-model RTLLM-v2 pass@5 values also differ between Tables 2 and 7. These definitions and protocols should be reconciled.

Results lack uncertainty estimates or repeated-training runs, limiting confidence in smaller PPA improvements and component differences. Overall, the functional gains and breadth of experiments are promising, but the PPA evaluation and reproducibility gaps require important revisions before a sound Findings recommendation.
